stories.title: U.S. bans DeepSeek from government agency systems amid AI rift with China
stories.summary: U.S. Department of Homeland Security has banned DeepSeek-related technology from federal civilian agency IT systems.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: U.S. bans DeepSeek from government agency systems amid AI rift with China
sources.text: The Trump administration banned Chinese AI startup DeepSeek from civilian U.S. government agencies, citing security concerns. The Department of Homeland Security on Monday made public the order requiring federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek-related technology from their IT systems and barring them from procuring DeepSeek products and services. The ban applies to federal civilian agency IT systems, including third-party products and services developed using the company's technology. The move comes amid intensifying geopolitical tensions between Washington and Beijing, with artificial intelligence emerging as a key battleground in the two countries' race for technological dominance. Asked about the U.S. move by Reuters, China's foreign ministry told the news agency that it would safeguard the rights and interests of its companies. Mao Ning, a ministry spokesperson, said that "China consistently opposes the over-generalization of national security as well as the politicization of science, technology and trade issues," the agency reported. The order, originally issued on July 24, applies to federal civilian agencies, including the Treasury, State and Justice departments, but it excludes the Department of Defense. Since DeepSeek burst onto the scene at the start of 2025, several U.S. government agencies have imposed various restrictions. Congress restricted the use of DeepSeek in intelligence community systems in December 2025. Earlier that year in March, U.S. Commerce Department bureaus told staff DeepSeek was banned on government devices, Reuters reported at the time. The Defense Information Systems Agency moved to block access to DeepSeek models in January 2025, according to reports from Bloomberg. DeepSeek's AI models "present multiple threat vectors," the latest DHS order states, citing concerns over potential access to sensitive data by Chinese authorities and potential cybersecurity vulnerabilities. The agency also warned that using DeepSeek's AI models could result in sensitive U.S. government data being transferred to China, potentially providing intelligence on American citizens and government programs. The models may also contain malware or other security vulnerabilities, the agency said, citing open-source research that identified multiple critical vulnerabilities in DeepSeek's iOS app. Executive agencies can request exceptions to the order, including delays in compliance, by submitting a written justification to the DHS within 60 days of the order's issuance. DeepSeek and China's Embassy in the U.K. did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

sources.name: The Guardian Technology
sources.title: US bans use of China’s DeepSeek AI tools by government agencies
sources.text: Use of tools ‘may result in the transfer of sensitive data’ to China, defense department says The US government on Monday ordered its agencies to stop using artificial intelligence (AI) tools from the Chinese startup DeepSeek , as the countries race for dominance in the fast-moving sector. A notice from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced the ban on products developed by DeepSeek – and tools created using DeepSeek by third parties – saying they must be removed from IT devices. The DHS can issue direction to civilian agencies but not the military or intelligence services. The US defense department did not respond to an AFP request for comment. “DeepSeek’s models present multiple threat vectors,” said a document attached to Monday’s notice. Use of DeepSeek AI tools “may result in the transfer of sensitive data to [China] if used by US government employees or vendors”, the department warned. Its servers are located in China, where the legal system permits the government “extensive authority” to access private company infrastructure, it said. One of China’s top AI labs, DeepSeek shook up the industry in January 2025 with a low-cost, high-performance chatbot, challenging assumptions of US dominance. The firm released a long-awaited new model, V4, in April, and earlier in October updated a faster, more lightweight version of V4. The US has accused DeepSeek and other top Chinese AI firms of systematically stealing the capabilities of cutting-edge models developed by American rivals. Despite their fierce competition in the field, when their leaders Xi Jinping and Donald Trump met at the White House in September, China and the US agreed to set up a “communication channel” for AI incidents. The topic is expected to arise again at a meeting between Xi and Trump at a summit scheduled for November in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

sources.name: TechCrunch AI
sources.title: US orders federal agencies to remove China’s DeepSeek AI from their systems
sources.text: The U.S. has ordered federal civilian agencies to stop purchasing services and products developed by Chinese AI startup DeepSeek and remove them from government IT systems over national security concerns tied to the Chinese AI startup’s operations in China, according to the Department of Homeland Security. The order goes beyond banning DeepSeek’s own product, but also covers third-party products and services built using DeepSeek technology, though agencies can request exceptions. The DHS raised concerns about DeepSeek’s handling of user data, warning that sensitive information from US government users could potentially be accessible to Chinese authorities under Chinese law, the order said . The move comes amid intensifying tech competition in AI between the US and China. The Chinese AI model challenges its U.S. rivals, including OpenAI and Meta, with low-cost open-weight models. China pushed back against the U.S.’s move. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Tuesday that Beijing opposes “overstretching the concept of national security and politicizing technology and trade issues,” according to an official briefing. “We will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises,” the spokesperson added. The U.S. has already taken steps to limit DeepSeek’s use in government. A law passed in December 2025 targeted its use in intelligence’s national security systems. The latest order extends the restrictions to federal civilian agencies, covering both new purchases and existing IT systems. Meanwhile, China is reportedly considering export restrictions on 23 AI-related technologies, including chip designs and certain advanced AI models, to address security and misuse risks, Bloomberg reported last week . The Chinese AI lab has faced scrutiny from governments and regulators across the globe since its R1 reasoning model shook the AI industry in January 2025, triggering a sharp sell-off in Nvidia shares. The U.S. accused DeepSeek and five other Chinese AI companies, including Alibaba and Moonshot AI, of using large-scale model distillation to extract information from American AI systems, according to a September report. In addition, OpenAI and Anthropic have separately raised concerns about DeepSeek’s alleged use of model distillation, a technique that uses outputs from one AI model to train another. Earlier this year, OpenAI told U.S. lawmakers it had observed suspected attempts by DeepSeek to distill its models, while Anthropic said it had identified unauthorized attempts by DeepSeek and other Chinese AI labs to collect outputs from Claude. sources.title: DeepSeek AI tools banned from US government agency systems as rift with China grows
sources.text: Federal civilian agencies are no longer allowed to use DeepSeek and must remove it from their tech stack The Donald Trump administration has banned Chinese Artificial Intelligence model DeepSeek from all civilian government agencies and ordered them to stop using it and remove it from its tech stack immediately. Earlier this week, the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued a new notice, notifying government agencies of the change: “The Department of Homeland Security is publishing notice of the Secretary of Homeland Security’s issuance of an order (1) excluding information technology products and services developed by Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co., Ltd (DeepSeek), to include affiliated entities as defined in applicable regulations, from federal civilian agency procurements; and, (2) removing all DeepSeek and DeepSeek-affiliate products, and third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations, from civilian agency information technology.” Apparently, this is not the first time the Trump administration made moves against Chinese AI tech. According to CNBC , the order was originally issued in late July this year, and applies to federal civilian agencies including the Treasury, State and Justice departments, but excluding the Department of Defense. The publication also said the US Congress restricted the use of DeepSeek in intelligence community systems late last year, and even earlier - in March - the US Commerce Department told its staff not to use DeepSeek. The Defense Information Systems Agency banned it in January 2025. In the latest DHS order, it was said that DeepSeek’s models “present multiple threat vectors”. To use the tool, users need to provide all sorts of data - from personally identifiable information (PII) to other business or proprietary information, which the company can use to “track and digitally fingerprint users”. Furthermore, China’s laws allow the government to easily access and collect the data created and stored by private companies, meaning information on US citizens can easily fall into the government’s hands. That, in turn, “could produce actionable intelligence on US persons and/or government programs,” the DHS explains. “The models themselves may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities,” it stressed. “Indeed, open-source security research has found that the DeepSeek iOS mobile application contains multiple critical vulnerabilities.” When asked for a comment, China’s foreign ministry told the Reuters news agency it would safeguard the rights of its companies: “China consistently opposes the over-generalization of national security as well as the politicization of science, technology and trade issues,” Mao Ning, a ministry spokesperson, told the agency. US President Donald Trump has openly talked against using Chinese technology and has banned multiple companies and solutions already. In his first term, he blacklisted hundreds of Chinese companies and affiliates, including telecommunications giants Huawei and ZTE, semiconductor manufacturer SMIC, drone maker DJI , and surveillance technology firms Hikvision and Dahua Technology. ZTE almost went bankrupt over it, and Huawei ended up building its own mobile phone operating system , Harmony OS, after losing access to Google and Android. At the time, the US was upgrading its mobile network to 5G, something Chinese companies were interested in working on. However, Trump argued that the Chinese government could force these companies into installing backdoors, which could allow China to eavesdrop on US communications. In August 2026, during his second term, Trump signed an executive order declaring a national emergency and banned all foreign bulk-power systems from being imported, installed, or used in the country. He also said the government would analyze existing systems to isolate and remove any foreign-built hardware or software. The same ban was issued during his first term but was revoked by the Biden administration. Later this month, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) will vote to prevent all Chinese labs from testing hardware used in the US, Reuters reported. stories.title: OpenAI acquires Orchestra Bio
stories.summary: OpenAI is acquiring Orchestra Bio to bring AI-powered operations to life sciences R&D, helping biopharma teams accelerate drug development and advance new treatments.

sources.name: OpenAI
sources.title: OpenAI acquires Orchestra Bio
sources.text: AI-powered drug development platform accelerates progress toward new treatments. OpenAI has acquired Orchestra Bio ⁠ (opens in a new window) , a platform that helps biopharma teams coordinate the complex process of drug development. We’re bringing Orchestra’s team and technology together with Rosalind , our AI models and tools for life sciences research. Our goal is to help scientists make discoveries and manage the work needed to turn them into treatments that reach patients sooner. Developing a new medicine is extraordinarily complex, taking roughly 10 to 15 years on average from target discovery to regulatory approval in the United States. Beyond the science, teams must orchestrate programs across internal departments and external partners, often relying on disconnected systems. We’re now at an inflection point where AI can help take on these specialized tasks and complex workflows. Rosalind brings our AI models and tools to life sciences researchers. GPT‑Rosalind helps scientists reason through questions in biology and chemistry. Rosalind Workbench ⁠ connects those capabilities with scientific tools and data to help researchers analyze results and plan experiments. Orchestra brings a team with experience across biotech, software, and AI, along with a platform built to coordinate drug development. Together, we aim to build agents that help teams connect scientific findings with the studies, decisions, and next steps needed to advance a potential medicine. Orchestra Bio is a platform where people and AI agents work together to advance drug programs. Scientists and program leaders delegate the monitoring and tracking of studies and campaigns to agents, freeing up time to guide the work, make decisions, and address issues before they cause delays. A problem in one part of a drug program can affect many others. A failed manufacturing batch, for example, can delay the start of a clinical trial. Orchestra’s agents help teams identify which activities and timelines are affected, gather the relevant information, and compare ways to respond. Scientists and program leaders can then use that analysis to decide what to do next. Realizing the potential of AI in life sciences requires close collaboration with the organizations working at the forefront of drug discovery and development. Our partnership with Novo Nordisk ⁠ aims to translate its scale and scientific expertise into faster R&D and commercial execution while maintaining strong governance. At Moderna ⁠ , AI is helping teams translate insights from complex data into experimental workflows, with the potential to accelerate R&D. Our vision is for AI to help scientists across the full process of discovering and developing new medicines: exploring ideas, designing experiments, interpreting results, and coordinating the work needed to advance promising treatments. Bringing Orchestra Bio together with Rosalind is a step toward that vision. Alongside researchers and our partners, we aim to make more discoveries possible and help new medicines reach patients sooner.

sources.name: TechCrunch AI
sources.title: OpenAI acquires startup Orchestra Bio⁠ to beef up its biotech business
sources.text: OpenAI on Tuesday acquired a four-year-old AI biotech software startup called Orchestra Bio, the company announced via its website. Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but the startup had reportedly raised around $20 million as of 2025 from backers like Andreessen Horowitz, Atria, and 8VC. Orchestra creates AI agents that help biotech companies manage the minutiae of drug discovery operations, from tracking finances to resolving scheduling issues with clinical trials. OpenAI says it’s adding Orchestra’s team and technology to work on Rosalind , its AI model for life sciences research, and to its related Rosalind Workbench tool, a harness that aims to help researchers plan experiments and analyze results. OpenAI has already won some big names as customers for Rosalind, including, it says, Moderna⁠ and Novo Nordisk⁠. The acquisition is a classic example of how the biggest AI labs (namely OpenAI and Anthropic) are building ever more software for the biggest industries, like pharma. In the startup world, there is an ongoing fear that at any moment, the labs will launch new features and become competitors. In this case, Orchestra is getting absorbed, rather than stomped out. stories.title: Anthropic commits 5% of shares to new public benefit fund that could address AI job disruption
stories.summary: The Claude maker said that establishing the fund as an LLC will provide greater flexibility in how the money is used.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: Anthropic commits 5% of shares to new public benefit fund that could address AI job disruption
sources.text: Anthropic said Sunday it plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund , with the stake potentially increasing as the company's valuation grows. Subject to shareholder approval, the fund would immediately commit 5% of Anthropic's shares, with the board adding, at its discretion, an additional 2% for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline that has yet to be disclosed. Anthropic said that while it has already committed $200 million to study the AI's effects, "given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed." The fund may be used to "explore large donations" — including to traditional nonprofits or as direct distributions for specific populations — or for "bolder approaches" to study and address AI's disruption and displacement of jobs, the company said. An August Pew Research Center report found that 71% of adults think AI will lead to fewer jobs in the U.S. over the next two years. The fund will be established as a wholly owned limited liability company rather than a 501(c)(3) tax-exempt nonprofit or other format to adjust between different forms of giving, the release said. Equity held by the LLC will not be used for lobbying or political giving in the U.S. or internationally, Anthropic said. Anthropic told investors its third-quarter revenue stands at $16.8 billion ahead of its planned initial public offering reportedly slated for November, CNBC reported . The timing of Anthropic's public fund announcement is both mandatory to prepare for an initial public offering, and "beneficial from an image perspective," especially as AI reshapes the jobs market, Lise Buyer, partner at IPO advisory firm Class V Group, told CNBC. Buyer said Anthropic's move could be seen favorably if the funds support retraining or help workers find alternative employment when the technology disrupts their jobs. "Of course, it is also to burnish their reputation at a time when AI is coming under significant scrutiny," she added. Anthropic said it will share more about the fund structure and governance in the coming months, including valuation milestones that may increase the stake. It said it will also share progress on the fund in an upcoming public benefit report. In response to Anthropic's announcement, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X that he "recommend[s] giving the shares directly to the public."

sources.name: The Guardian Technology
sources.title: AI firm Anthropic to commit 5% of shares to fund for ‘public good’
sources.text: The $48bn giveaway comes amid concerns about the tech and as the company prepares for a stock market listing Anthropic has said it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund for the “public good”, as the AI developer behind the Claude chatbot seeks to bolster its appeal before its stock market listing. The company announced it would commit the shares, worth around $48bn (£36bn) at its latest valuation in May, subject to shareholder approval. It will add a further 2% of its stock to the fund for every 50% increase in its value above an undisclosed baseline. The fund will allow Anthropic to “explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations”, the company said. The move comes amid growing public nervousness about AI, from the threat to human labour to the impact on the environment and its influence on social behaviours. “AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers,” Anthropic wrote in a blogpost. It said that while it had already committed $200m to addressing the issue, “given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The fund will have the versatility to pursue them.” The company, which is preparing to list on the stock market, has called for a slowdown in breakneck development of AI, a warning later echoed by rivals such as OpenAI. Anthropic was valued at $965bn in May when it raised $65bn in a funding round. The company is reportedly considering a $1.5tn valuation when it floats on the stock market, with an IPO planned for November. Last week, Anthropic said some of its AI models could soon become “self-replicating” and find ways to infiltrate internet-connected devices such as smart fridges and automatic vacuum cleaners. It said that once this happens, the models would be able to power themselves without the need of datacentres. Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and founder of SpaceX, responded to Anthropic’s plans for a public benefit fund on social media by pledging to give some of his own shares away. “I recommend giving the shares directly to the public,” he wrote. “This is what I will be doing.” He later announced: “Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many.” Shares in SpaceX, which is listed on the Nasdaq in the US, rose by 1% in pre-market trading on Monday. The company has lost about 9% of its value since it joined the stock market in June. OpenAI, the developer behind ChatGPT, also reportedly engaged in early talks to give a 5% stake in its organisation to the US government . Anthropic, which was founded in 2021 by seven former OpenAI employees, was established as a public benefit corporation. It means that all of the company’s directors must balance financial returns with its public interest mission.
